question.text: The CVaR (Expected Shortfall) at 95% of a portfolio is Rs. 3 cr. This means:

answer.text: The portfolio will lose Rs. 3 cr 95% of the time
Given that losses exceed the 95% VaR, the EXPECTED loss is Rs. 3 cr
There is a 5% probability of losing exactly Rs. 3 cr
The minimum loss at 95% confidence is Rs. 3 cr

explanation.text: The Logic: Conditional VaR (also called Expected Shortfall) is the expected loss given that the loss has already exceeded the VaR threshold. At 95% confidence, CVaR averages losses across the worst 5% of outcomes. A CVaR of Rs. 3 cr therefore says: in the tail beyond the 95% VaR cut-off, the average loss is Rs. 3 cr. The Trap: '95% of the time' confuses a frequency with a tail expectation; '5% probability of losing exactly Rs. 3 cr' treats an average as a point probability; the 'minimum loss at 95% confidence' definition actually describes VaR, not CVaR. Note: The NISM-Series-XXI-B workbook chapter on risk (pp. 289-300, plus pp. 315 and 371-379) uses 'CVaR' to mean Credit VaR in the credit-risk context and does not define Expected Shortfall / Conditional VaR in the pages checked. The framing above reflects the general industry definition of Expected Shortfall used by Basel-aligned risk practitioners.
